identity.title: Dynamic auscultation: systolic murmur louder with Valsalva/standing, softer with squatting or handgrip

technique.how: Listen at the left sternal border/apex, then have the patient strain (Valsalva) for 10-20 s and note whether the murmur gets louder; repeat while the patient rises from squatting to standing (louder = positive) and from standing to squatting (softer = positive). Sustained handgrip for 20-30 s should soften an HCM murmur.
technique.prerequisites: Patient able to stand and squat safely with assistance; baseline murmur already characterised.
technique.contraindications: Avoid Valsalva and squat-stand in patients with recent syncope, unstable angina, severe orthostasis, or fall risk without assistance.

interpretation.positive_finding: A murmur that increases with Valsalva or on standing and decreases with squatting or handgrip identifies dynamic LVOT obstruction (HCM) with high specificity (Valsalva 96%, standing 84-85%); Valsalva-louder gives a computed LR+ of about 16.
interpretation.negative_finding: A murmur that does not increase with squat-to-stand or does not decrease with stand-to-squat makes HCM unlikely (sensitivity 95%, computed LR- ~0.06); murmurs of valvular AS soften or stay unchanged with Valsalva and are not identified by any single manoeuvre.
interpretation.pitfalls: Valsalva has low sensitivity for HCM (65%); poor technique (short strain, incomplete squat) blunts responses; mitral valve prolapse murmurs also become longer/louder on standing; data come from one 50-patient referral cohort with cardiologist examiners.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: suspect HCM - order echocardiography, avoid dehydration, nitrates and inotropes; negative squat/stand response argues for fixed obstruction (AS) or regurgitant lesions.

estimates.target_condition: Hypertrophic (obstructive) cardiomyopathy murmur vs all other systolic murmurs
estimates.population: 50 patients with documented systolic murmurs of defined cause (HCM, AS, MR, VSD, right-sided lesions, MVP), examined by cardiologists
estimates.reference_standard: Echocardiography/Doppler and catheterization-confirmed etiology of the murmur (as described in study)
estimates.computed_from: LR+ = 0.65/(1-0.96) = 16.25; LR- = (1-0.65)/0.96 = 0.36; from abstract-reported sensitivity 65% and specificity 96% (increase in intensity with Valsalva).
estimates.quote: an increase in intensity with the Valsalva maneuver (65 percent sensitivity, 96 percent specificity)
estimates.location: Abstract, Results (PubMed abstract; NEJM full text not accessible)

sources.citation: Lembo NJ, Dell'Italia LJ, Crawford MH, O'Rourke RA. Bedside diagnosis of systolic murmurs. N Engl J Med. 1988;318(24):1572-1578.
Etchells E, Bell C, Robb K. Does this patient have an abnormal systolic murmur? JAMA. 1997;277(7):564-571.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not perform Valsalva/squat-stand manoeuvres in patients with recent syncope, hemodynamic instability, active ischaemia, or inability to stand safely; do not use to exclude non-obstructive HCM (no murmur to augment).
safety_scope.escalation_warning: A Valsalva-augmented murmur in a patient with exertional syncope, chest pain or a family history of sudden death needs prompt echocardiography and cardiology referral; avoid dehydration, vasodilators and beta-agonists meanwhile.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Reliability of manoeuvre responses not reported by Lembo 1988; underlying murmur detection has fair reliability (kappa 0.30-0.48, RCE 1997). All estimates are from cardiologist examiners in a single 50-patient referral series.

extraction_notes: All numbers are from the Lembo 1988 NEJM abstract (n=50; no CIs reported in the abstract; full text not accessible, so the study's table numbers/2x2 cells were not seen). LRs computed by me from the abstract sensitivity/specificity and flagged computed=true. Setting recorded as 'mixed' because the abstract does not state inpatient vs outpatient. The 1997 RCE summarises HCM manoeuvre studies as 'smaller, lower-quality' but its abstract gives no HCM numbers, so it is cited as context only. Passive leg elevation (85%/91%) omitted as not part of this record's title. No pooled/meta-analytic estimate for dynamic auscultation was found in PubMed searches.
